english: Acme, Septimius, his loves,
note: amores: his beloved (plural for singular); Acmen is object of tenens on the next line.

latin: tenens in gremio mea, inquit, Acme,
english: holding in his lap, my, he said, Acme,

latin: ni te perdite amo atque amare porro
english: unless I love you desperately and to love henceforth
note: perdite: to the point of ruin; porro: further on in time.

english: all I am constantly ready the years
note: omnes ... annos: through all the years.

english: as much as one who can most greatly perish,
note: perire: to be dying of love; quantum qui pote: as much as anyone can.

english: alone in Libya and scorched India
may I come face to face with a grey-eyed lion.
note: veniam: subjunctive of a curse on himself; caesius: blue-grey (of eyes).

latin: hoc ut dixit, Amor, sinistra ut ante,
english: When he said this, Love, on the left as before,
note: sinistra ut ante, dextra: sense disputed; as printed, Love, who before (sneezed) on the left, now sneezed on the right.

english: on the right sneezed approval.
But Acme, lightly her head bending back
and the sweet boy's drunken little eyes
with that crimson mouth having kissed,
note: purpureus: deep red, glowing.

english: So, she said, my life, little Septimius,
note: Septimille: diminutive of Septimius.

english: to this one master continually let us be slaves,
note: serviamus: hortatory subjunctive; the master is Love.

english: as much greater for me and fiercer
note: ut: 'as (surely as)', an oath formula; multo: by far.

english: a fire burns in my soft marrow.
note: medullae: marrow, the innermost body; possessive supplied.

latin: hoc ut dixit, Arnor, sinistra ut ante,
english: When she said this, Love, on the left as before,
note: The source prints 'Arnor', a misprint for Amor; kept unchanged in the Latin field.

english: on the right sneezed approval.
Now from a good omen having set out
note: auspicium: bird-sign, omen.

english: with mutual hearts they love, are loved.
the one Acme Septimius, poor wretch,
note: misellus: poor little (lovesick) fellow.

english: prefers rather than Syrias and Britains:
note: plurals: all the Syrias and Britains, i.e. rich provincial posts.

english: in Septimius alone faithful Acme
makes her delights and lusts.
note: libidines: desires, sexual pleasures.

english: Who any men more blessed
has seen, who a Venus more auspicious?
note: Venus: a love; auspicatior: begun under better omens.

english: Now spring brings back the unchilled warmths,
note: egelidos: with the chill gone.

english: now the fury of the equinoctial sky
at the pleasant breezes of Zephyr grows silent.
Let the Phrygian plains be left, Catullus,
note: linquantur: jussive subjunctive.

english: and the fertile field of sweltering Nicaea:
to the bright cities of Asia let us fly.
note: claras: bright, famous.

english: Now the mind, trembling beforehand, longs to wander,
now glad with eagerness the feet grow strong.
O sweet gatherings of companions, farewell,

latin: longe quos simul a domo profectos
english: whom, together, far from home having set out,
note: quos: masculine plural, the companions of the coetus.

english: different, varied roads carry back.
Porcius and Socration, two left hands
note: sinistrae: the left hand is the thief's hand, i.e. Piso's thieving agents.

english: of Piso, scab and famine of the world,
you, to my little Veranius and to Fabullus,
note: Veraniolo: diminutive of Veranius.

english: has that circumcised Priapus preferred?
note: verpus: circumcised, or with foreskin drawn back (erect); obscene abuse of their patron.

english: You, banquets elegant, sumptuously
from daytime make? my comrades
note: de die: starting while it is still day, a mark of luxury.

english: seek on the crossroad invitations?
note: trivium: the meeting of three roads, the street corner.

english: Your honeyed eyes, Iuventius,
if someone were to let me continually kiss,
note: sinat: subjunctive.

english: continually up to three hundred thousand I would kiss,
note: basiem: subjunctive.

english: nor ever would I seem to be going to be sated,
not if denser than the dry ears of grain
were the crop of our kissing.
Most eloquent of the descendants of Romulus,

latin: quot sunt quotque fuere, Marce Tulli,
english: as many as are and as many as were, Marcus Tullius,

latin: quotque post aliis erunt in annis,
english: and as many as afterwards in other years will be,
the greatest thanks to you Catullus
gives, the worst poet of all,
by so much the worst poet of all
by as much as you the best advocate of all.
note: patronus: patron, advocate in court; 'of all' can mean 'advocate of anybody', a possible double edge.

english: Yesterday, Licinius, at leisure
much we played on my tablets,
note: tabellae: wax writing tablets.

english: as it had been agreed to be dainty.
note: delicatos: self-indulgent, playful.

english: writing little verses each of us

latin: ludebat numero modo hoc modo illoc,
english: was playing in metre now this, now that,
note: numero: in rhythm, metre.

latin: reddens mutua per iocum atque vinum.
english: giving back in turn through joke and wine.
note: mutua: replies in exchange.

english: And I went away from there by your charm
set on fire, Licinius, and by your witticisms,
note: possessive supplied with facetiis.

latin: ut nec me miserum cibus iuvaret,
english: so that neither food would help wretched me,
note: iuvaret: subjunctive of result.

english: nor sleep cover with quiet my little eyes,
but over the whole, untamed by frenzy, bed
note: toto ... lecto: over the whole bed.

english: I would toss, longing to see the light,

latin: ut tecum loquerer simulque ut essem.
english: so that I might talk with you and at the same time be with you.
note: ut essem: 'that I might be (together)'; 'with you' carried from tecum.

english: But, worn out with toil, after my limbs
note: postquam: after; possessive supplied.

english: half-dead on the little bed were lying,
this, delightful one, for you I made, poem,
note: i.e. this poem I made for you.

english: from which you might perceive my pain.

latin: nunc audax cave sis, precesque nostras,
english: Now, beware of being bold, and our prayers,
note: cave sis audax: take care you are not bold (rash).

english: we pray, beware of spitting out, little eye,
note: ocelle: little eye, i.e. darling; despuere: to spit upon, reject.

latin: ne poenas Nemesis reposcat a te.
english: lest Nemesis demand back penalties from you.

latin: est vehemens dea: laedere hanc caveto.
english: She is a violent goddess: beware of offending her.
note: caveto: future imperative.

latin: Ille mi par esse deo videtur,
english: That man seems to me to be equal to a god,

latin: ille, si fas est, superare divos
english: that man, if it is right, to surpass the gods,
who, sitting opposite, again and again you
watches and hears
sweetly laughing, which, wretched, all
note: quod: neuter, 'a thing which', referring to the whole scene; misero agrees with mihi on line 6.

latin: eripit sensus mihi: nam simul te,
english: senses snatches from me: for as soon as you,

latin: Lesbia, adspexi, nihil est super mi
english: Lesbia, I have looked at, nothing is left over to me
note: super: left over (in reserve).
Gap: a line is lost in the manuscripts (often supplied as 'vocis in ore', of voice in my mouth).

latin: lingua sed torpet, tenuis sub artus
english: but the tongue grows numb, thin beneath the limbs
a flame flows down, with their own sound
ring the ears, by twin are covered
note: gemina ... nocte: by twin night.

english: the lights night.
note: lumina: lights, i.e. the eyes; gemina nocte: with a double night.

english: Idleness, Catullus, to you is troublesome:
in idleness you exult and too much you run riot.
note: gestis: you are wildly eager, carried away.

latin: otium et reges prius et beatas
english: Idleness both kings before and blessed
has ruined cities.

latin: Quid est, Catulle? quid moraris emori?
english: What is it, Catullus? Why do you delay to die?

latin: sella in curuli struma Nonius sedet,
english: In the curule chair the tumour Nonius sits,
note: struma: a scrofulous swelling, goitre; abuse of Nonius.

english: by the consulship Vatinius swears falsely:
note: perierat: read as peierat 'perjures himself' (swears by his promised consulship); taken as a pluperfect of pereo it would be 'had perished'.

latin: quid est, Catulle? quid moraris emori?
english: What is it, Catullus? Why do you delay to die?

latin: Risi nescio quem modo e corona,
english: I laughed at someone just now from the ring,
note: corona: crown, the ring of bystanders at a trial.

english: who, when wonderfully the Vatinian
my Calvus charges had set out,
note: Vatiniana crimina: the charges against Vatinius.

english: marvelling says these things and his hands raising:
Great gods, the eloquent little prick!
note: salaputium: word of uncertain meaning; most likely an obscene diminutive 'little cock' (manikin), applied to the short Calvus.

english: Otho's head is exceedingly tiny,

note: Gap marker in the source; the poem is fragmentary and its order uncertain.

english: and of Erius the rustic half-washed legs,
note: eri: corrupt or a name (Herius, Nerius); could also be 'of the master'.

english: the fine and light fart of Libo,
note: peditum: fart; subtile et leve: thin and quiet.
Gap marker in the source.

english: if not all, I would wish to displease
note: vellem: subjunctive.

english: you and Fuficius, re-cooked old man
note: recoctus: boiled again, i.e. rejuvenated (as Medea boiled Aeson).
Gap marker in the source.

english: you will be angry again at my iambics
note: irascere: future 'you will be angry', or imperative 'be angry'.

english: undeserving, unique commander.
note: immerentibus: undeserving (of anger), with iambis; unice imperator: Caesar.

latin: Oramus, si forte non molestum est,
english: We beg, if perhaps it is not troublesome,
that you show where are your darknesses.
note: tenebrae: darkness, i.e. hiding-place.

english: You in the lesser Field we have sought,
note: campus minor: a lesser Campus in Rome.

latin: te in circo, te in omnibus libellis,
english: you in the Circus, you in all the little books,
note: libelli: perhaps the booksellers' stalls.

latin: te in templo summi Iovis sacrato.
english: you in the temple of highest Jupiter, consecrated.
in Magnus's at the same time promenade
note: Magnus: Pompey; his colonnade.

english: all the little women, friend, I seized,
whom with face I saw nevertheless serene.
note: quas: feminine plural, the women.

english: † A velte thus I myself kept demanding:
note: Corrupt: 'A velte' between cruces is left untranslated; conjectures include 'avelte' and 'a vel te'.

english: Camerius to me, you most wicked girls!
note: camerium: the source has lower case; the name Camerius.

english: a certain one, she says, naked † reduc †
note: Corrupt; often restored 'nudum reducta pectus', drawing back her bare breast; quaedam is feminine.

latin: en hic in roseis latet papillis.
english: look, here in rosy little nipples he lies hidden.
note: papillae: nipples, breasts.

latin: sed te iam ferre Herculi labos est:
english: But to bear you now is a labour for Hercules:
note: Merrill prints lines 23-32 (often numbered 58b) at this point; the records keep that order.

latin: Non custos si fingar ille Cretum,
english: Not if I were fashioned that guardian of the Cretans,
note: custos Cretum: Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete. Lines 23-32 are the piece often printed as 58b.

english: not if on Pegasean flight I were borne,
not if I Ladas or wing-footed Perseus,
note: Ladas: a famous runner; 'if' carried from the series of 'non si'.

english: not if Rhesus's snowy and swift two-horse team:
add here the feather-footed and the flying,
and of the winds at the same time ask the running,
note: require: ask for, seek.

english: which, bound, Camerius, to me you might dedicate:
note: quos: masculine plural, the winds and winged ones; dicares: subjunctive.

english: worn out nevertheless in all my marrows
note: medullae: marrow, inmost being.

english: and by many languors eaten up
I would be, you for myself, friend, by seeking.
note: quaeritando: by searching (for you); essem: subjunctive.

english: with such great disdain do you deny yourself, friend?
note: ten = tene, you (with question particle).

latin: dic nobis ubi sis futurus, ede
english: tell us where you are going to be, declare
boldly, entrust, trust to the light.
Now do milk-white girls hold you?

latin: si linguam clauso tenes in ore,
english: If the tongue in a closed mouth you keep,
the fruits you will throw away of love all:
in wordy chatter Venus delights.

latin: vel vi vis, licet obseres palatum,
english: or, if you wish, you may bolt your palate,
note: The source prints 'vi vis', likely for 'si vis' (if you wish); the doubtful text is kept in the Latin field.

english: provided that you be a sharer of true love.
note: sis: subjunctive.

latin: O rem ridiculam, Cato, et iocosam
english: O thing laughable, Cato, and jocular
and worthy of the ears and of your guffaw.
Laugh, as much as you love, Cato, Catullus:
note: quidquid amas: however much you love (Catullus).

latin: res est ridicula et nimis iocosa.
english: the thing is laughable and too jocular.
I caught just now a little boy, of a girl
note: pupulum puellae: a girl's little boy, or puellae dative with trusantem (thrusting at a girl).

latin: trusantem: hunc ego, si placet Dionae,
english: thrusting: him I, if it pleases Dione,
note: trusare: to thrust repeatedly, sexual intercourse; Dione: mother of Venus.

english: instead of a weapon with my stiff one I struck.
note: rigida mea: my stiff (cock), feminine for mentula; cecidi from caedo 'strike', here sexual: I fucked him.

english: Finely it fits the shameless catamites,
note: cinaedi: men who take the passive role in anal sex; convenit: there is agreement between.

english: Mamurra and the buggered one and Caesar.
note: pathicus: one who is anally penetrated; with -que ... -que it may describe Mamurra, Caesar or both.

english: Nor a wonder: stains equal for both,
one of the city and that of Formiae,
note: Mamurra came from Formiae.

english: stamped in, remain and will not be washed out:
diseased equally, twins both,
note: morbosus: diseased, sexually perverted.

english: in one little couch, little scholars both,
note: eruditulus: learned little one; double sense with the couch.

latin: non hic quam ille magis vorax adulter,
english: not this one than that more greedy an adulterer,
partner rivals of little girls:
Finely it fits the shameless catamites.
Caelius, our Lesbia, that Lesbia,
that Lesbia, whom Catullus alone
note: quam: feminine, Lesbia.

latin: plus quam se atque suos amavit omnes,
english: more than himself and his own all loved,
now at crossroads and in alleys
note: quadrivium: meeting of four roads.

english: peels the great-souled grandsons of Remus.
note: glubit: peels, strips bark; obscene: she skins back their foreskins, jerks them off.

english: Bononian Rufa sucks off Rufulus,
note: fellat: fellates.

latin: uxor Meneni, saepe quam in sepulcretis
english: wife of Menenius, whom often in the graveyards
note: quam: feminine, Rufa.

latin: vidistis ipso rapere de rogo cenam,
english: you have seen snatch from the very pyre her dinner,
note: food left for the dead was burned on the pyre.

latin: cum devolutum ex igne prosequens panem
english: when, following the bread rolled down out of the fire,
by a half-shaven corpse-burner she was being beaten.
note: ustor: one who burns corpses; tunderetur: subjunctive in a cum clause.

english: Surely not you a lioness in the Libystine mountains
note: num: expects the answer no; Libystinus: Libyan.

latin: aut Scylla latrans infima inguinum parte
english: or Scylla, barking in the lowest part of her groins,
note: possessive supplied; inguina: groin, where Scylla's dogs grew.

latin: tam mente dura procreavit ac taetra,
english: with a mind so hard begot and foul,

latin: ut supplicis vocem in novissimo casu
english: that a suppliant's voice in his latest plight
note: novissimus casus: last extremity.

latin: contemptam haberes, ah nimis fero corde?
english: despised you would hold, ah, with too fierce a heart?
note: haberes: subjunctive of result.
